word:hebrew:H1077.explanation: Bal means not or not at all; it is a negating word used when an action or condition is denied.

word:hebrew:H1095.explanation: Belteshatstsar is the Babylonian name given to Daniel.

word:hebrew:H1118.explanation: This word refers to “Bimhal,” a personal name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. It functions as the name of an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament and appears once, in 1 Chronicles 7:33. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, no further meaning or significance should be assigned beyond identifying the person named. Its use is therefore proper-name usage, not a general vocabulary term.

word:hebrew:H113.explanation: Adon means a sovereign or controller, whether human or divine. It can refer to a human master in relation to a servant or to a king addressed as lord.

word:hebrew:H1143.explanation: Benayim means the space between two armies. It can also mean a champion.

word:hebrew:H1240.explanation: Bᵉqar means to search. It can also mean to inquire about a matter.

word:hebrew:H1305.explanation: Barar means to clarify, examine, or select. It can describe making words clear, testing people, or choosing people for service.

word:hebrew:H1446.explanation: Gedor names a place and is also used as a personal name.

word:hebrew:H1514.explanation: Gaham is a personal name, referring to an individual named in the Hebrew Old Testament. It appears once, in Genesis 22:24, within a genealogical record. word:hebrew:H1561.explanation: Gêlel means dung, or dung in ball-like form.

word:hebrew:H16.explanation: Abeh means papyrus. In one biblical use, it is rendered as “swift.”

word:hebrew:H1622.explanation: Girgashi means a Girgashite, one of the native tribes of Canaan.

word:hebrew:H1727.explanation: This Hebrew word means “pine.” It is a verb describing a person’s condition or experience rather than naming an object. Because it appears only there and the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding wording. word:hebrew:H1859.explanation: Dar means an age or generation.

word:hebrew:H1860.explanation: This Hebrew word means “contempt.” As a noun, it names the condition of being regarded with scorn or dishonor. It occurs only twice in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 66:24 and Daniel 12:2, so its meaning is seen in these two closely related passages rather than across many settings. In Isaiah, the word is connected with death and what is seen afterward, highlighting a rejected and dishonored condition. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H1965.explanation: Heikal means a palace. It can also mean a temple.

word:hebrew:H1987.explanation: Helem is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Helem.” It identifies a person in the Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears once in the Hebrew Bible, at 1 Chronicles 7:35. Because the available information preserves the name but does not provide a separate definition, its ordinary biblical function is simply to distinguish this individual from others. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain Helem’s particular identity or family connection there.

word:hebrew:H2025.explanation: This Hebrew word is a unique biblical term whose precise meaning cannot be securely stated from the lexical information available. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 43:15. Because no approved English meaning or definition is provided, assigning a specific translation, spiritual idea, or contextual force would go beyond what can be established. Its meaning must be understood from Ezekiel 43:15 and the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H2111.explanation: Zûwaʻ means to move or tremble, and can also describe being vexed.

word:hebrew:H2164.explanation: The word means “prepared”: it describes someone or something made ready for what is about to happen. In its Hebrew Old Testament use, it functions as a verb, expressing readiness rather than naming a person, place, or object. It occurs twice, both within Daniel 2:9, so its broader range cannot be established from this small number of occurrences. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H2281.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “pans,” naming utensils used in a practical household or service setting. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 9:31. Since the word appears only in that single location and no verse text is available here, its broader contextual force cannot be described beyond this basic meaning. The singular lexical idea identifies a specific kind of vessel rather than an action, person, or quality.

word:hebrew:H2366.explanation: Hushim is a personal name referring to a person in Israel’s genealogical records. It is rendered “Hushim” and occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. Its uses are connected with family lines and records of birth or begetting, so it identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s specific role in each passage.

word:hebrew:H2388.explanation: Chazaq means to seize or hold fast. It can also describe being strong or courageous, being strengthened, or being firmly established. It may also mean to repair.

word:hebrew:H2410.explanation: Hatita is a Hebrew name, functioning as a designation rather than a descriptive word. It occurs twice in the Old Testament corpus, once in Ezra 2:42 and once in Nehemiah 7:45. The same name is rendered “Hatita” in the available English renderings. Since no explicit lexical definition is available, its meaning is best understood as the name itself, while the surrounding verse determines whom it identifies.

word:hebrew:H2429.explanation: Chayil can refer to an army or to strength.

word:hebrew:H2623.explanation: Chasid describes a godly or holy person. It can also describe someone as merciful.

word:hebrew:H265.explanation: Ahoah is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, at 1 Chronicles 8:4, and is rendered “Ahoah.” Because no explicit definition is given for this name, its significance cannot be expanded beyond identifying the person named in that genealogy. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

word:hebrew:H2696.explanation: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Hezron.” It identifies a person in the Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. Hezron appears in genealogical records and family lists, where the name marks an individual within Israel’s ancestry. The name occurs 18 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Genesis, Numbers, Joshua, Ruth, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding genealogy or narrative.

word:hebrew:H2757.explanation: Charits means something cut or sliced. It can also refer to a harrow.

word:hebrew:H2803.explanation: Chashab means to devise or contrive. It can also mean to reckon or count something. It may also mean to regard or consider something as valuable.

word:hebrew:H2858.explanation: This Hebrew word means “signet,” referring to an identifying seal or stamped object. A signet could represent its owner when presented or shown, so the word points to something connected with personal identification and authority. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Genesis 38:25. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the signet is being used there.

word:hebrew:H287.explanation: Ahimoth is a personal name, referring to a specific man rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs only once, and English Bible translations preserve it as “Ahimoth.” The available passage reference is 1 Chronicles 6:25, but the surrounding verse text is not provided here, so the name itself does not support further conclusions about the person or his role. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the proper name Ahimoth in that genealogical record.

word:hebrew:H2955.explanation: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Taphath.” It functions as a proper name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 4:11, and is rendered “Taphath” in the available English renderings. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical role is to identify a person by name.

word:hebrew:H3167.explanation: Jahaziah is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Jahaziah,” rather than a term describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies one person in the Old Testament and appears once, in Ezra 10:15. The available form establishes the person’s name, but this single occurrence does not establish an additional lexical meaning or broader concept. Its precise significance as a personal name therefore remains unstated here.

word:hebrew:H3185.explanation: Jahziel is a personal name, rendered “Jahziel,” rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament and appears once, in 1 Chronicles 7:13. Since no explicit definition or broader usage is recorded, the name should be understood primarily as the person’s designation, not expanded into an unverified meaning. Its significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogy.

word:hebrew:H3206.explanation: Yeled means something born, such as a child or offspring. It can also refer to a young man, and in other contexts to children.

word:hebrew:H3475.explanation: Jesher is the name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H3497.explanation: Ithnan is a Hebrew proper name rendered in English as “Ithnan.” It functions as a name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joshua 15:23. Because it is preserved as a name and no broader definition is given, its meaning cannot be expanded beyond identifying the named individual or place in that passage.

word:hebrew:H3556.explanation: Kowkab means a star, a shining object in the heavens. Scripture also uses stars to picture a great multitude.

word:hebrew:H359.explanation: Eloth is the name of a place on the Red Sea.

word:hebrew:H3673.explanation: Kânash means to assemble or gather together.

word:hebrew:H3750.explanation: Karkom means the crocus, or saffron.

word:hebrew:H3893.explanation: The Hebrew word means “natural.” It is a descriptive term, marking something as belonging to the ordinary or inherent condition of a person or thing, rather than something added or unusual. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Deuteronomy 34:7. Its exact force in that verse is determined by the surrounding wording, but its basic contribution is to identify what is natural or inherent.

word:hebrew:H409.explanation: Al means not; it marks a prohibition, as in “Destroy not.”

word:hebrew:H4250.explanation: This Hebrew word is a family or clan name referring to the “Mahlites.” It identifies a particular Israelite group in genealogical lists rather than describing an action, quality, or object. word:hebrew:H4269.explanation: Machsom means a muzzle or bridle for restraining the mouth.

word:hebrew:H430.explanation: Elohim means God when it refers to Yahweh, the supreme God. It can also mean gods when referring to foreign deities.

word:hebrew:H4328.explanation: This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Ezekiel 41:8. word:hebrew:H4373.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to a counted amount or an assigned worth—“number” or “valuation.” It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Exodus and once in Leviticus. In one setting, it concerns determining a number; in the other, it functions as something whose value is assessed in connection with giving. Thus, the word centers on an amount established by counting or appraisal, rather than describing the act of counting itself. Its exact emphasis depends on the sentence where it occurs.

word:hebrew:H4467.explanation: Mamlakah means a kingdom or realm. It can also describe a dominion, a realm under a ruler’s authority.

word:hebrew:H4562.explanation: This Hebrew noun means “bond,” referring to something that binds or holds people together. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Ezekiel 20:37. The word’s basic sense identifies a binding connection, while the surrounding passage determines exactly how that bond functions in the verse. Its single occurrence makes it a specialized term in the Hebrew biblical corpus rather than a frequently repeated word.

word:hebrew:H4706.explanation: Mitsar means a peak of Lebanon and appears as Mizar in English.

word:hebrew:H4801.explanation: Merchaq means remoteness or a distant place. It can also describe being far away, as when something comes from afar.

word:hebrew:H4874.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to something involved in the debt-related instruction of Deuteronomy 15:2. Its exact everyday meaning cannot be stated more narrowly from the available lexical information, because no definition or approved meaning term is preserved here. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 15:2, and functions there as the object of several relationships involving the whole matter being addressed. Its precise sense therefore depends on the wording and context of that verse.

word:hebrew:H4908.explanation: This Hebrew noun refers to the “tabernacle,” the designated dwelling place associated with Israel’s worship. It names the sacred structure that was made, arranged, and set up according to God’s instructions, rather than an ordinary home or building. The word appears 139 times in the Old Testament corpus, especially in Exodus and Numbers, where the tabernacle is central to Israel’s ordered worship and service. Its normal scriptural use therefore points to this particular sanctuary and its furnishings as Israel’s appointed place of meeting with God.

word:hebrew:H492.explanation: This Hebrew word means “such,” pointing to a person or thing of the kind already under discussion without naming it directly. It functions as a descriptive reference rather than a personal name or specific title. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, appearing once each in Ruth, 1 Samuel, and 2 Kings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic function is to identify someone or something by kind or description.

word:hebrew:H4953.explanation: Mashroqi means a flute or musical pipe.

word:hebrew:H5037.explanation: Nabal is the personal name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H5194.explanation: Neta means a plant. It can also refer to planting.

word:hebrew:H5200.explanation: Netophathi means a Netophathite, or an inhabitant of Netophah.

word:hebrew:H5239.explanation: Nalah means to complete or make an end.

word:hebrew:H5576.explanation: Sancherib is the name of an Assyrian king. English renderings use Sennacherib for this name.

word:hebrew:H5598.explanation: Sippai is a Hebrew personal name, written as “Sippai,” rather than a word that expresses an action, quality, or object. word:hebrew:H5604.explanation: Sippun means a wainscot or ceiling.

word:hebrew:H5671.explanation: This Hebrew word means “thick.” It functions as a descriptive word, telling the reader what something is like rather than naming an action, person, or object. word:hebrew:H5752.explanation: Oded is the name of two Israelites.

word:hebrew:H5891.explanation: Ephah is a personal name. It names a son of Midian and can also name a region associated with Midian.

word:hebrew:H6065.explanation: This Hebrew word means “confiscation”—the taking of property by an authority, usually as an official penalty or legal action. It functions as a term describing property being seized rather than voluntarily given. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 7:26. word:hebrew:H6087.explanation: ʻAtsab means to grieve. It can also mean to cause pain.

word:hebrew:H6159.explanation: Oreb is a personal name. It names a Midianite prince and also the rock where he was killed.

word:hebrew:H6160.explanation: Arabah means a desert, especially a valley or plain.

word:hebrew:H6313.explanation: Pûwg means to be sluggish. It can also describe being weak or faint.

word:hebrew:H6348.explanation: This Hebrew word means “light.” It describes someone or something as light in character or conduct rather than identifying a physical object. In the Old Testament, it appears only twice, once in Judges and once in Zephaniah, and both occurrences are rendered “light.” Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but its basic idea is a quality or description applied to a subject.

word:hebrew:H6483.explanation: This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It is a Hebrew word whose ordinary English meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information alone. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 24:15. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise action or reference should be understood from that passage rather than guessed from the word by itself.

word:hebrew:H6502.explanation: Piram is a personal name identifying an individual, rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, at Joshua 10:3, and is rendered “Piram.” Because the available material contains no short definition beyond this name, its meaning is best understood as its identifying function: it names a particular person in the biblical account. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its full text.

word:hebrew:H6599.explanation: This Hebrew noun refers to an official “decree” or “sentence”—a formal decision issued with authority. It names something that can be made or given, functioning as the object of those actions. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, rendered “decree” in Esther 1:20 and “sentence” in Ecclesiastes 8:11. Its central idea is an authoritative ruling or pronouncement, rather than an ordinary statement or personal opinion.

word:hebrew:H6609.explanation: Pethichah means something opened, referring to a drawn sword.

word:hebrew:H6630.explanation: Tsaʼănân is the name of a place in Palestine.

word:hebrew:H6818.explanation: Tsaʻăqâh means a shriek or cry. It may be the cry of afflicted people under oppression, heard by Yahweh.

word:hebrew:H683.explanation: Atsaljah is the name of an Israelite, rendered Azaliah in English.

word:hebrew:H6843.explanation: Tsᵉphîyrâh means a crown or diadem. It can also refer to a turn of affairs or mishap, appearing as “morning” in warnings of approaching trouble.

word:hebrew:H6977.explanation: Qevutstsah means a forelock or lock of hair, especially hair shorn or cut.

word:hebrew:H7008.explanation: Qiytor means a fume or cloud, including smoke or vapor.

word:hebrew:H7053.explanation: Qilleshon means a prong or hay-fork, rendered as a fork.

word:hebrew:H7101.explanation: Qatsin means a magistrate or other leader. It can describe a captain over men of war or a ruler over people.

word:hebrew:H7174.explanation: Karkor is the name of a place. It is a Hebrew proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Judges 8:10, and the English translations represented here preserve it as “Karkor.” Without the surrounding verse text, its specific setting and significance cannot be explained further; the lexical evidence identifies it as a place name only.

word:hebrew:H7219.explanation: Rosh means poison or a poisonous substance, including gall or venom.

word:hebrew:H7220.explanation: Rosh is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or command. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Genesis 46:21, and the English rendering preserves it as “Rosh.” Because this word appears only in that single occurrence and no broader definition is provided, its clearest ordinary sense is the name itself. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H7282.explanation: Ragea means restful or peaceable, and can describe those who are quiet.

word:hebrew:H7347.explanation: Rêcheh means a millstone, a stone used for grinding.

word:hebrew:H7426.explanation: Ramam means to rise, literally or figuratively.

word:hebrew:H7493.explanation: Raash means to shake or tremble. It can describe the earth trembling.

word:hebrew:H7624.explanation: Shebach means to praise or adore.

word:hebrew:H7651.explanation: Sheba means seven. It can also express seven times, as in “sevenfold.”

word:hebrew:H7732.explanation: Shobal is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Shobal.” It identifies people named in Israel’s genealogical records rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in genealogical passages in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. Its recorded use includes family relationships and lines of descent, so its normal function is to name a person within a genealogy. The surrounding verse determines which individual named Shobal is intended.

word:hebrew:H7790.explanation: Shûwr means a foe—an enemy lying in wait.

word:hebrew:H7875.explanation: Sîyd means lime. It can also refer to plaster used to coat stones.

word:hebrew:H7897.explanation: Shith means a dress or attire, something put on.

word:hebrew:H7956.explanation: Shelah is a personal name. Shelah is named as Judah’s son, and a family line is traced from him.

word:hebrew:H8023.explanation: This Hebrew word means “Shiloni” and functions as a personal name or identifying designation. It is not presented here as an action, quality, or command, but as a name attached to someone or something identified in the text. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Nehemiah 11:5. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise referent must be determined from that passage rather than from the name alone.

word:hebrew:H805.explanation: Ashurite means an inhabitant of the district of Ashur. Asshurim is the collective name for the Ashurites.

word:hebrew:H8096.explanation: Shim‘i is a personal name; English translations render it Shimei.

word:hebrew:H8157.explanation: Sheçaʻ means a fissure or cleft, and in animal descriptions it refers to a hoof that is split or cloven-footed.

word:hebrew:H8210.explanation: Shaphak means to pour out or shed. It describes blood being shed or poured out. It can also describe casting up a mound or a soul being poured out figuratively.

word:hebrew:H8229.explanation: Shipha means abundance. It can also describe a multitude. It can also refer to a company.

word:hebrew:H8481.explanation: Tachtown means bottommost, the lowest position. It can also describe something lower or nethermost.

word:hebrew:H8588.explanation: Taănûwg means luxury. It can describe something delicate. It can refer to delights. It can also describe what is pleasant.

word:hebrew:H8625.explanation: This word means “TEKEL,” a distinctive term preserved in the biblical text rather than ordinarily rendered as a descriptive English word. It functions as a named or displayed word in Daniel 5, appearing three times across two verses. Because its precise lexical sense is not given here beyond this preserved term, it is best understood first as the word “TEKEL” itself; its particular force in each occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:hebrew:H940.explanation: Buzite means a descendant of Buz; Elihu is identified as a Buzite.

word:hebrew:H979.explanation: Bᵉchurôwth means youth and can also refer collectively to young men.
